messages.author: 7919e430d76b4f9e
messages.subject: VHF Data & Bootstrapping
parts:
Hi Chris, 

Thanks so much for creating this package! I am really interested in using it to produce home ranges for my dataset. 

I am working with VHF telemetry data (triangulated using sigloc) and I have small datasets (15-45 points per individual). The small sample sizes were part  of the reason why I was drawn to your package. 

I have worked through the vignettes and found them extremely helpful. However, when I work through using my own data, I run into some problems. I used ctmm.select with the pHREML method due to my small sampling size. However, I only get appropriate DOF values (4-5) for 2/29 individuals. I assume this is due to the nature of my data - I have max. 1 location per day. 

Is it appropriate to bootstrap this type of data? Do you have any other ideas for me for how to produce an appropriate model? I am an M.Sc. student and it is my first time venturing into this field. 

Thank you so much for your time. 

Best, 

Isabella Richmond

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: VHF Data & Bootstrapping
parts:
Hi Isabella,

The first thing I would say is that, unless your animals move very far compared to the triangulation error, to make sure you get your error ellipses imported into ctmm. (See discussion here: https://groups.google.com/forum/?oldui=1#!searchin/ctmm-user/VHF$20error$20ellipse|sort:date/ctmm-user/TrLypiFqG7E/fuiHCi7eFgAJ ) Unfortunately, I haven't streamlined this process because I intend to eventually support triangulation within ctmm using an estimator slightly better than the one used by sigloc, which is no longer on CRAN.

If 27/29 individuals have DOF[area] estimates less than 4-5, then I would definitely consider a parametric bootstrap to improve the home-range estimates. Also, I would consider
  • Is the improved DOF[area] estimate from ctmm.boot (with an error target small enough to resolve DOF[area] numerically, like error=0.001 or something) within the range that you would expect the resulting home-range estimate to be reliable (2-3)? If not, I would still do it, but report that you don't expect those estimates to be very good.
  • We're doing some simulation analysis comparing the different estimators for an overview paper, and from those not-yet-published results I would recommend iterate=TRUE, as it seems to perform slightly better on average than the default (and faster) iterate=FALSE. I will probably change the default argument in the next version of the package.
Best,
Chris

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: VHF Data & Bootstrapping
parts:
Hi Isabella,

You are running into the same issue that Chris was. Some of your error ellipses have negative variances. Both of you guys are/were using sigloc, so I assume either the issue is with sigloc or with the estimator that sigloc is based on.

For instance, the 3rd individual's 12th time has error ellipse

         x        y
x 37546.68 30190.13
y 30190.13 23520.29

which when fed into eigen() reports

eigen() decomposition
$values
[1] 61527.5030  -460.5261

$vectors
           [,1]       [,2]
[1,] -0.7830312  0.6219824
[2,] -0.6219824 -0.7830312

That second eigenvalue is a variance of -460.5261 square meters, which is impossible.

I suppose there are 3 possible solutions.
  1. Lazy solution: Drop all times with negative variances.
  2. Figure out if there is some way to prevent this in sigloc. Maybe there is a numerical error argument that can be clamped down or something. I'm not familiar with the package.
  3. If this is just numerical error, then you could fix the small, negative eigenvalue to zero, with some code like below. This would be more-or-less correct if the negative variances are just small numerical errors.
If EVD=eigen(COV), then

EVD$vectors %*% diag(EVD$values,2) %*% t(EVD$vectors)

should return back the original COV matrix estimate, and

EVD$vectors %*% diag(pmax(EVD$values,0),2) %*% t(EVD$vectors)

returns a matrix with zero variance substituted for the negative variance, which in this case is

         [,1]     [,2]
[1,] 37724.84 29965.84
[2,] 29965.84 23802.66

and is the same to almost 3 digits.

Best,
Chris

On Friday, June 26, 2020 at 2:51:39 PM UTC-2:30 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi Isabella,

The first thing I would say is that, unless your animals move very far compared to the triangulation error, to make sure you get your error ellipses imported into ctmm. (See discussion here: https://groups.google.com/forum/?oldui=1#!searchin/ctmm-user/VHF$20error$20ellipse|sort:date/ctmm-user/TrLypiFqG7E/fuiHCi7eFgAJ ) Unfortunately, I haven't streamlined this process because I intend to eventually support triangulation within ctmm using an estimator slightly better than the one used by sigloc, which is no longer on CRAN.

If 27/29 individuals have DOF[area] estimates less than 4-5, then I would definitely consider a parametric bootstrap to improve the home-range estimates. Also, I would consider
  • Is the improved DOF[area] estimate from ctmm.boot (with an error target small enough to resolve DOF[area] numerically, like error=0.001 or something) within the range that you would expect the resulting home-range estimate to be reliable (2-3)? If not, I would still do it, but report that you don't expect those estimates to be very good.
  • We're doing some simulation analysis comparing the different estimators for an overview paper, and from those not-yet-published results I would recommend iterate=TRUE, as it seems to perform slightly better on average than the default (and faster) iterate=FALSE. I will probably change the default argument in the next version of the package.
Best,
Chris

On Saturday, July 4, 2020 at 9:48:13 PM UTC-2:30, Christen Fleming wrote:
Hi Isabella,

You are running into the same issue that Chris was. Some of your error ellipses have negative variances. Both of you guys are/were using sigloc, so I assume either the issue is with sigloc or with the estimator that sigloc is based on.

For instance, the 3rd individual's 12th time has error ellipse

         x        y
x 37546.68 30190.13
y 30190.13 23520.29

which when fed into eigen() reports

eigen() decomposition
$values
[1] 61527.5030  -460.5261

$vectors
           [,1]       [,2]
[1,] -0.7830312  0.6219824
[2,] -0.6219824 -0.7830312

That second eigenvalue is a variance of -460.5261 square meters, which is impossible.

I suppose there are 3 possible solutions.
  1. Lazy solution: Drop all times with negative variances.
  2. Figure out if there is some way to prevent this in sigloc. Maybe there is a numerical error argument that can be clamped down or something. I'm not familiar with the package.
  3. If this is just numerical error, then you could fix the small, negative eigenvalue to zero, with some code like below. This would be more-or-less correct if the negative variances are just small numerical errors.
If EVD=eigen(COV), then

EVD$vectors %*% diag(EVD$values,2) %*% t(EVD$vectors)

should return back the original COV matrix estimate, and

EVD$vectors %*% diag(pmax(EVD$values,0),2) %*% t(EVD$vectors)

returns a matrix with zero variance substituted for the negative variance, which in this case is

         [,1]     [,2]
[1,] 37724.84 29965.84
[2,] 29965.84 23802.66

and is the same to almost 3 digits.

Best,
Chris
